prompt: A generated suggestion compiles without complaint. What does that establish?
optionA: That it works correctly
optionB: That it is well formed, and nothing about whether it does the right thing
optionC: That it matches what was asked for
optionD: That it has been checked
correctAnswerText: That it is well formed, and nothing about whether it does the right thing
explanation: Compiling is a statement about form. Code that computes entirely the wrong answer compiles just as readily as code that computes the right one.

prompt: A suggestion arrives with a clear explanation of how it works. What has the explanation established?
optionA: That the author understood the problem
optionB: That the code matches the explanation
optionC: That the code has been tested
optionD: Nothing on its own; it was produced the same way the code was
correctAnswerText: Nothing on its own; it was produced the same way the code was
explanation: The explanation is another piece of generated text rather than a report on the code. Whether the two agree is something a reader has to check.

prompt: What is the status of a generated suggestion before anyone has examined it?
optionA: A proposal that has not been checked
optionB: A working solution
optionC: A draft that is probably wrong
optionD: A solution that works for the common case
correctAnswerText: A proposal that has not been checked
explanation: It is neither established as right nor established as wrong. Assuming either without looking is what the review exists to prevent.

prompt: A developer accepts a suggestion without reading it, reasoning that it can be reverted if it turns out to be wrong. What does that reasoning overlook?
optionA: That reverting is technically difficult
optionB: That the suggestion cannot be reverted once accepted
optionC: That a wrong result may not announce itself, so there may be nothing prompting a revert
optionD: Nothing; reverting is a sufficient safeguard
correctAnswerText: That a wrong result may not announce itself, so there may be nothing prompting a revert
explanation: Reverting answers the case where the fault is noticed. The suggestions worth worrying about are the ones that produce plausible wrong answers quietly.

prompt: A developer refuses to use generated suggestions at all, on the grounds that they cannot be trusted. What is wrong with that position?
optionA: Nothing; generated code should never be used
optionB: Unverified is not the same as wrong; the suggestion needs checking rather than refusing
optionC: Generated suggestions are correct often enough to accept without checking
optionD: The position is right for code and wrong for tests
correctAnswerText: Unverified is not the same as wrong; the suggestion needs checking rather than refusing
explanation: Blanket refusal and blanket acceptance are the same error with the sign reversed: both replace looking at the code with a policy about where it came from.

prompt: A developer asks for a function returning the second largest value in a list. The suggestion sorts the list and returns the second element. Does it meet the requirement?
optionA: Yes, sorting then taking the second is correct
optionB: Yes, provided the list has no duplicates
optionC: It cannot be decided without running it
optionD: No; it returns the second smallest
correctAnswerText: No; it returns the second smallest
explanation: Sorting puts the smallest first, so the second element is the second smallest. The code is well written and answers a different question.

prompt: A developer asks for a function that removes duplicates while keeping the original order. The suggestion removes duplicates and returns the values sorted. Does it meet the requirement?
optionA: No; the ordering requirement was not met
optionB: Yes, since the duplicates were removed
optionC: Yes, since sorting is a reasonable ordering
optionD: It depends on whether the input was already sorted
correctAnswerText: No; the ordering requirement was not met
explanation: Half the requirement was met and the other half was replaced with something else. Sorted is an order and not the order that was asked for.

prompt: A suggestion is well written, clearly named and correctly indented, and computes a total that includes tax where the requirement said to exclude it. Should it be accepted?
optionA: Yes, since the style shows it was carefully produced
optionB: Yes, with a comment noting the difference
optionC: No; the style is good and the behaviour is wrong
optionD: It cannot be decided without seeing the tax rate
correctAnswerText: No; the style is good and the behaviour is wrong
explanation: Presentation and behaviour are independent. Well-written code that computes the wrong figure is harder to reject precisely because it looks finished.

prompt: A reviewer rejects a suggestion because it uses a loop where the team usually uses a built-in operation. The behaviour is exactly what was requested. Is the rejection about the requirement?
optionA: Yes; using the wrong construct means the requirement was not met
optionB: No; it is about house style, which is a separate matter from meeting the requirement
optionC: Yes; house style is part of every requirement
optionD: No, and style objections should never be raised
correctAnswerText: No; it is about house style, which is a separate matter from meeting the requirement
explanation: The style point may well be worth making and is not a requirement failure. Confusing the two makes review feedback impossible to prioritise.

prompt: A suggestion calls a method named parseFlexibleDate on a date library. Which part of the suggestion most needs checking before use?
optionA: Whether the variable names follow house style
optionB: Whether the indentation is consistent
optionC: Whether the call is on its own line
optionD: Whether that method exists in the library
correctAnswerText: Whether that method exists in the library
explanation: A plausible method name is exactly what generation produces, and one that does not exist fails only when the code runs. Layout can be checked at a glance and costs nothing if wrong.

prompt: A suggestion reads naturally and uses a helper called ensureSortedUnique that nobody on the team recognises. What follows?
optionA: It has to be looked up, since reading naturally is not evidence that it exists
optionB: It exists, since the code would not have been produced otherwise
optionC: It does not exist, since nobody recognises it
optionD: It exists but has been renamed
correctAnswerText: It has to be looked up, since reading naturally is not evidence that it exists
explanation: Neither conclusion follows from recognition. The name is plausible whether or not there is anything behind it, which is the whole difficulty.

prompt: Why is a fabricated function name particularly easy to miss when reading a suggestion?
optionA: Because it is usually hidden in a comment
optionB: Because it is usually spelled unusually
optionC: Because it is named the way a real one would be
optionD: Because it appears only in rarely executed branches
correctAnswerText: Because it is named the way a real one would be
explanation: Naming things plausibly is what the process is good at. A fabricated name looks exactly like the name the library ought to have had.

prompt: A suggestion uses a method that turns out not to exist. A developer asks the generator whether the method exists, and is told that it does. What has been established?
optionA: That the method exists and the documentation is incomplete
optionB: Nothing; the second answer was produced the same way as the first
optionC: That the method exists in a newer version
optionD: That the developer searched incorrectly
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the second answer was produced the same way as the first
explanation: Confirming a claim by the process that produced it is not a check. The library documentation or the code itself is what settles the question.

prompt: A developer asks for a function that returns the average of a list of numbers. The suggestion divides the total by the count. What did it decide that the request did not specify?
optionA: Which arithmetic operation to use for an average
optionB: Whether the numbers are whole or fractional
optionC: Whether to name the function average
optionD: What to do when the list is empty
correctAnswerText: What to do when the list is empty
explanation: An empty list makes the count zero, and the request never said what should happen. The suggestion has taken a position on it without saying so.

prompt: A developer asks for a function that finds a user by email address. The suggestion compares the addresses exactly as given. What has it decided silently?
optionA: That the comparison should distinguish upper and lower case
optionB: That the function should return one user rather than several
optionC: That email addresses are strings
optionD: That the search should be fast
correctAnswerText: That the comparison should distinguish upper and lower case
explanation: Email addresses are commonly treated as case-insensitive, and the request did not say. Taking the simpler comparison is a decision that will show up as users not being found.

prompt: A suggestion returns the first item of a list that matches a condition. Which input would it not handle correctly?
optionA: A list where everything matches
optionB: A list with exactly one item
optionC: A list where nothing matches
optionD: A list already in order
correctAnswerText: A list where nothing matches
explanation: With nothing matching there is no first item to return, and the request never said what should happen. The other three all have a clear first match.

prompt: A suggestion splits a full name into a first and last name by taking the text before and after the first space. Which input would it handle wrongly?
optionA: A name with two parts
optionB: A name with three parts, where the middle part joins the surname
optionC: A name written in capitals
optionD: A name with a hyphen in the surname
correctAnswerText: A name with three parts, where the middle part joins the surname
explanation: Three parts leave the middle name attached to the surname, which is silently wrong. A hyphen contains no space and is handled correctly.

prompt: A reviewer suspects a suggestion mishandles an empty list. Which test settles it?
optionA: Call it with a list of one item
optionB: Call it with a long list
optionC: Read the code again more carefully
optionD: Call it with an empty list and see what happens
correctAnswerText: Call it with an empty list and see what happens
explanation: The doubt names a specific input, so that input is the test. The other calls would pass whether or not the doubt is justified.

prompt: A reviewer suspects a suggestion returns the second smallest value rather than the second largest. Which test distinguishes the two?
optionA: A list whose second smallest and second largest values differ
optionB: A list of two identical values
optionC: A list already sorted in increasing order
optionD: A list of five identical values
correctAnswerText: A list whose second smallest and second largest values differ
explanation: The test has to be an input where the two behaviours give different answers. Identical values make the two indistinguishable, which is exactly what a test must not do.

prompt: A reviewer suspects a suggestion treats email addresses as case-sensitive when it should not. A test using two addresses that differ in case would behave differently depending on whether the suspicion is right, and one using identical addresses would not. Which test settles it?
optionA: Search for an address using exactly the case it was recorded in
optionB: Search for an address that is not in the records at all
optionC: Search for an address recorded in one case using the other case
optionD: Search for two different addresses in turn
correctAnswerText: Search for an address recorded in one case using the other case
explanation: Only the first produces different results under the two behaviours. Searching in the recorded case succeeds either way and would be read as evidence that nothing is wrong.

prompt: A developer asks for a function that doubles every number in a list, giving the example [1, 2, 3] to [2, 4, 6]. The suggestion adds each number to itself and matches the example. Is it correct in general?
optionA: No; it only works for the example given
optionB: Yes; adding a number to itself is doubling it for every number
optionC: No; it will fail for negative numbers
optionD: It cannot be decided without more examples
correctAnswerText: Yes; adding a number to itself is doubling it for every number
explanation: The method is different from the obvious one and is equivalent for every number, including negatives and zero. Not every unexpected approach is a fault.

prompt: A developer asks for a function that reports whether a year is a leap year, giving 2024 as an example. The suggestion returns true whenever the year divides by four, and is right about 2024. Is it correct in general?
optionA: Yes; divisibility by four is the rule
optionB: No; it will be wrong for every year after 2100
optionC: Yes, for any year in the current century
optionD: No; years divisible by 100 but not by 400 are exceptions it gets wrong
correctAnswerText: No; years divisible by 100 but not by 400 are exceptions it gets wrong
explanation: The example is one of the many years the simple rule handles correctly. The rule fails on 1900 and 2100, which the example could never have revealed.

prompt: A developer asks for a function returning the largest value in a list, with the example [3, 9, 4] giving 9. The suggestion returns the last value after sorting, and matches the example. Sorting places the largest value last, so the method is equivalent to taking the largest for every list. What follows?
optionA: It is correct in general, though it does more work than necessary
optionB: It is correct only for the example given
optionC: It is wrong, since it sorts rather than searching
optionD: It is wrong for lists containing duplicates
correctAnswerText: It is correct in general, though it does more work than necessary
explanation: The approach is inefficient and correct, and those are separate findings. Rejecting it for correctness would be a wrong review comment on working code.

prompt: A team stores all money as whole numbers of the smallest currency unit. A suggestion introduces a fractional value to hold a price. What is the problem?
optionA: Fractional values are always wrong for money
optionB: The suggestion is too slow
optionC: It uses a representation the rest of the codebase does not, so values will not combine correctly
optionD: Nothing; the two representations are interchangeable
correctAnswerText: It uses a representation the rest of the codebase does not, so values will not combine correctly
explanation: The suggestion is sound in isolation and inconsistent here. Mixing the two representations is where the errors arrive.

prompt: A team handles every failure by returning a result object describing what went wrong. A suggestion raises an exception instead. What is the difficulty?
optionA: Exceptions are always the wrong approach
optionB: Callers in this codebase inspect returned results and will not be handling exceptions
optionC: The suggestion will not compile
optionD: Nothing; both approaches signal failure
correctAnswerText: Callers in this codebase inspect returned results and will not be handling exceptions
explanation: Both are legitimate ways of reporting failure and the surrounding code only handles one. The exception will travel further than anyone expects.

prompt: A suggestion is technically correct and uses a naming style unlike the rest of the file. A reviewer wants to know how seriously to take this. The naming differs from the file and the behaviour matches the requirement exactly. How should it be recorded?
optionA: As a correctness problem, since consistency is a requirement
optionB: As nothing at all, since naming does not affect behaviour
optionC: As grounds for rejecting the suggestion entirely
optionD: As a style point worth fixing, kept separate from whether the code is correct
correctAnswerText: As a style point worth fixing, kept separate from whether the code is correct
explanation: Naming matters and does not make the code wrong. Grading every observation as a defect makes the genuinely broken things harder to see.

prompt: A suggestion arrives with the note "this handles the empty case by returning zero". The code contains no check for an empty input. What follows?
optionA: The explanation describes something the code does not do
optionB: The code handles it implicitly, as the note says
optionC: The note refers to a different version of the code
optionD: The note is correct and the code should be trusted
correctAnswerText: The explanation describes something the code does not do
explanation: The note and the code disagree, and the code is what runs. That the note sounds reassuring is why the disagreement is worth looking for.

prompt: A suggestion is described as "sorting the list in place to avoid allocating a copy". The code produces a new sorted list and leaves the original untouched. What is the consequence?
optionA: No consequence; both approaches sort the list
optionB: The code is faster than described
optionC: The original is unchanged, so any caller relying on the described behaviour will be wrong
optionD: The code will fail to compile
correctAnswerText: The original is unchanged, so any caller relying on the described behaviour will be wrong
explanation: A caller who believed the note would expect the original to be sorted afterwards, and it is not. The code may be preferable and it is not what was advertised.

prompt: A suggestion is accompanied by a clear, plausible and internally consistent explanation. The code does exactly what the explanation says. The explanation and the code agree with each other, and neither has been compared against the stated requirement. What has been established?
optionA: That the code is correct
optionB: That the two agree; nothing yet about whether either meets the requirement
optionC: That the code meets the requirement
optionD: That the explanation was written by someone who understood the task
correctAnswerText: That the two agree; nothing yet about whether either meets the requirement
explanation: Agreement between the two rules out one class of fault and not the one that matters most. Both can describe the same wrong behaviour perfectly.

prompt: A suggestion adds a line to a script that runs once, prints a report, and is read by the person who ran it. What most needs establishing before accepting?
optionA: That the code follows the team naming conventions
optionB: That the code would work at a much larger scale
optionC: That every branch has a test
optionD: That the printed figures are right, which the reader will see immediately
correctAnswerText: That the printed figures are right, which the reader will see immediately
explanation: The consequence of an error here is a wrong number in front of someone who is looking at it. The checks worth making are the ones proportionate to that.

prompt: A suggestion changes how refunds are calculated in a system that issues thousands of refunds a day with nobody reviewing them individually. What most needs establishing?
optionA: That the calculation is right for the awkward cases, since nobody will notice if it is not
optionB: That the code is readable
optionC: That the change is small
optionD: That the code runs quickly enough
correctAnswerText: That the calculation is right for the awkward cases, since nobody will notice if it is not
explanation: Volume and the absence of a reader are what raise the stakes here. A wrong refund calculation will be applied thousands of times before anyone notices.

prompt: Two suggestions are up for acceptance. One changes a log message. One changes how a customer balance is computed. Both are equally well written and equally short. One of the two would produce wrong figures for customers if it were incorrect, and the other would produce a confusing log line. How should the checking effort be divided?
optionA: Equally, since both are equally short
optionB: Equally, since both are equally well written
optionC: Overwhelmingly onto the balance calculation, because of what a wrong result would cost
optionD: Onto the log message, since logs are read more often
correctAnswerText: Overwhelmingly onto the balance calculation, because of what a wrong result would cost
explanation: Length and quality of writing say nothing about consequence. What a mistake would cost is what decides how much checking is worth doing.

prompt: A suggestion computes a running total. Line 1: set total to zero. Line 2: for each item in the list. Line 3: set total to the item price. Line 4: return total. It returns the price of the last item rather than the sum. Which line is responsible?
optionA: Line 1, which starts the total at zero
optionB: Line 3, which replaces the total instead of adding to it
optionC: Line 4, where the wrong value is returned
optionD: Line 2, which visits the items in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: Line 3, which replaces the total instead of adding to it
explanation: Replacing rather than adding is the whole fault, and it reads almost identically to the correct version. Line 4 is where the wrong value becomes visible rather than where it arises.

prompt: A suggestion filters a list and reports the count. Line 1: set matches to an empty list. Line 2: for each item in the input. Line 3: if the item is active, add it to matches. Line 4: return the length of the input. The count returned is always the size of the whole input. The returned length is taken from the input rather than from the list that was built. Which line is responsible?
optionA: Line 3, where the condition is wrong
optionB: Line 1, which starts with an empty list
optionC: Line 2, which visits every item rather than only the active ones
optionD: Line 4, which measures the wrong list
correctAnswerText: Line 4, which measures the wrong list
explanation: Everything up to the last line is correct and the result is discarded. The fault reads naturally because both lists are in scope and either name would look reasonable there.

prompt: A developer asks for a function to be made faster. The rewrite is faster and now returns results in sorted order, where the original preserved input order. What has changed beyond the request?
optionA: The order of the results, which nobody asked to change
optionB: Nothing; the function is simply faster
optionC: The speed, which was what was requested
optionD: The names of the variables
correctAnswerText: The order of the results, which nobody asked to change
explanation: Speed was requested and ordering was not. Any caller depending on the original order is now broken by a change that was described as an optimisation.

prompt: A developer asks for a function to be tidied. The rewrite is shorter, clearer, and now raises an error for negative input where the original returned zero. The request was to tidy the function, and the behaviour for negative input has changed as well. How should this be judged?
optionA: It is an improvement and should be accepted
optionB: It is irrelevant, since tidying often changes details
optionC: The change to negative-input behaviour is unrequested and has to be decided deliberately
optionD: It is a fault in the rewrite and should be reverted without discussion
correctAnswerText: The change to negative-input behaviour is unrequested and has to be decided deliberately
explanation: Raising on negative input may well be better than returning zero, and that is a decision nobody made. Improvements smuggled into a tidying change are the hardest to argue against and the easiest to miss.

prompt: A suggestion is run once with a typical input and produces the right answer. What does that establish?
optionA: That it is right in general
optionB: That it is right for that input
optionC: That it is right for every typical input
optionD: Nothing at all
correctAnswerText: That it is right for that input
explanation: One passing run is real evidence about exactly one input. Extending it to inputs nobody tried is the step that has to be resisted.

prompt: A suggestion passes every test in an existing suite. The suite was written before the feature the suggestion implements. The suite contains no test exercising the new behaviour. What does passing establish?
optionA: That the suggestion is correct
optionB: That the suite is inadequate and should be rewritten
optionC: That the new behaviour works, since nothing failed
optionD: That the suggestion has not broken what was already covered; nothing about the new behaviour
correctAnswerText: That the suggestion has not broken what was already covered; nothing about the new behaviour
explanation: Passing an unrelated suite is a genuine and narrow result: no regression. The new behaviour has not been examined by anything.

prompt: A developer asks the generator to write tests for its own suggestion, and every test passes. The tests were produced from the same understanding of the task as the code, so a misunderstanding would appear in both. What has been established?
optionA: Little; a misunderstanding in the code would be reproduced in the tests
optionB: That the code is correct, since the tests pass
optionC: That the tests are correct, since they pass
optionD: Nothing whatever, so generated tests are worthless
correctAnswerText: Little; a misunderstanding in the code would be reproduced in the tests
explanation: Generated tests do catch careless slips and cannot catch a wrong reading of the requirement. Tests written from the requirement by someone else are what close that gap.

prompt: A team accepts suggestions only when a reviewer can state what the code does without reading the accompanying explanation. Stating what the code does without the explanation requires reading the code itself rather than a description of it. What does this rule achieve?
optionA: It slows review down without adding anything
optionB: It guarantees the code is correct
optionC: It forces the reviewer to read the code rather than the description of it
optionD: It replaces the need for tests
correctAnswerText: It forces the reviewer to read the code rather than the description of it
explanation: The rule targets the specific failure of reviewing the explanation instead of the code. It guarantees nothing about correctness and it removes one way of being fooled.

prompt: A suggestion has been read, tested on three inputs including the awkward ones, and checked against the requirement. A developer says it is now proven correct. Testing three inputs establishes the behaviour on those three and leaves every other input unexamined. Is that right?
optionA: Yes; reading, testing and checking together constitute proof
optionB: No; it is well evidenced rather than proven, and the distinction matters for what comes next
optionC: No; nothing short of exhaustive testing is evidence
optionD: Yes, provided the three inputs were well chosen
correctAnswerText: No; it is well evidenced rather than proven, and the distinction matters for what comes next
explanation: The work done is substantial and proportionate, and it is not proof. Treating it as proof is what stops anyone adding a test when a new case appears later.

prompt: Four tasks are candidates for generation. Converting a data file between two formats where the output can be compared against the input; naming variables in a private script; choosing an encryption scheme; estimating a project timeline. One of these produces a result that can be checked mechanically against something already known. Which is safest to delegate?
optionA: Choosing the encryption scheme, since it is well-documented territory
optionB: Estimating the timeline, since estimates are approximate anyway
optionC: Naming the variables, since names cannot be wrong
optionD: Converting the data file, since the result can be compared against the input
correctAnswerText: Converting the data file, since the result can be compared against the input
explanation: Checkability rather than difficulty is what decides. An encryption choice that is subtly wrong is both consequential and hard for a beginner to detect.

prompt: A student is learning to write loops and asks a generator to write the loops in their coursework. The coursework exists to demonstrate that the student can write loops, and a generated loop demonstrates nothing about the student. What is wrong?
optionA: The generator has supplied the very thing the work exists to demonstrate
optionB: Nothing; using available tools is sensible
optionC: The loops will be wrong and will need correcting
optionD: The generator is unsuitable for loops specifically
correctAnswerText: The generator has supplied the very thing the work exists to demonstrate
explanation: The same request would be entirely reasonable in a job where the loops are a means to an end. What the work is for is what settles it.

prompt: A developer delegates a task they could not do themselves and could not check. The result looks reasonable. Neither producing the result nor evaluating it is within the developer reach, so nothing about it can be confirmed. What is the position?
optionA: A great deal has been gained, since the task is now done
optionB: The result should be accepted and monitored in use
optionC: Nothing has been gained that can be relied on, since the result cannot be evaluated
optionD: The result is probably wrong and should be discarded
correctAnswerText: Nothing has been gained that can be relied on, since the result cannot be evaluated
explanation: This is the case where delegation is most tempting and least defensible. Learning enough to evaluate it, or asking someone who can, is what turns the output into something usable.

prompt: A team can generate a first draft of a migration script in two minutes and would spend two hours writing it. Reviewing the generated draft carefully takes ninety minutes. The migration runs once against production data and cannot be undone. Reviewing takes ninety minutes against two hours of writing, and the migration cannot be undone. What follows?
optionA: Generating saves two hours, since the draft arrives in two minutes
optionB: Generating still saves time, provided the ninety-minute review actually happens
optionC: Generating saves nothing, since reviewing takes nearly as long
optionD: The script should be written by hand because the stakes are high
correctAnswerText: Generating still saves time, provided the ninety-minute review actually happens
explanation: The saving is thirty minutes rather than two hours, and it is real. It becomes a loss the moment the review is skipped because the draft looked fine.

prompt: A team forbids generated code in one repository and permits it in another. The forbidden one holds safety-critical control code reviewed line by line by two engineers. The permitted one holds internal reporting scripts. Both repositories are reviewed, and only one of them has consequences that a review might not catch. Is the distinction reasonable?
optionA: No; if review is trusted in one place it should be trusted in both
optionB: No; generated code should be forbidden everywhere
optionC: Yes, because reporting scripts are not really code
optionD: Yes; the two differ in what an undetected error would cost
correctAnswerText: Yes; the two differ in what an undetected error would cost
explanation: Both are reviewed and review is not perfect, which is why the residual risk differs. Applying one policy to both would either over-restrict the reports or under-protect the control code.

prompt: A developer receives a suggestion in a language they cannot read. They can run it and they know exactly what the correct output is for several inputs. The developer cannot read the code and can determine the correct output independently for several inputs. What is the most useful step?
optionA: Run it on those inputs and compare against the outputs they already know
optionB: Ask the generator to confirm that the code is correct
optionC: Accept it, since it cannot be reviewed
optionD: Reject it, since it cannot be reviewed
correctAnswerText: Run it on those inputs and compare against the outputs they already know
explanation: Not being able to read the code removes one form of checking and leaves another intact. Knowing the right answers independently is what makes the run informative.

prompt: A developer cannot read a suggestion and cannot determine the correct output for any input. They ask the generator to explain the code and find the explanation convincing. The explanation was produced by the same process as the code and is not evidence about it. What has been established?
optionA: That the code does what the explanation says
optionB: That the code is correct, since the explanation is coherent
optionC: Nothing; a convincing explanation from the same source is not a check
optionD: That the developer now understands the code
correctAnswerText: Nothing; a convincing explanation from the same source is not a check
explanation: This is the single most attractive wrong move in the whole skill, because it feels exactly like verification. Finding a person who can read the language is what actually helps.

prompt: A developer working in unfamiliar territory receives a suggestion using three constructs they do not recognise. They have time to investigate one. The three constructs differ in what a misunderstanding of each would cost if it were wrong. Which should they investigate?
optionA: The first one that appears in the code
optionB: The one whose being wrong would matter most
optionC: The one that looks most unusual
optionD: The shortest one, since it can be checked quickest
correctAnswerText: The one whose being wrong would matter most
explanation: Limited time is spent where the consequence is greatest rather than where curiosity points. Looking unusual is not correlated with mattering.

prompt: A team adopts a rule that any generated code touching money must be reproduced independently by a second person before acceptance, while other generated code needs one reviewer. Reproducing the work independently catches a misunderstanding that a reviewer reading the same code might share. What does the stricter rule buy?
optionA: Nothing beyond what careful review already provides
optionB: A guarantee that the money code is correct
optionC: Faster review, since two people work in parallel
optionD: Protection against a shared misreading, which reviewing the same code cannot provide
correctAnswerText: Protection against a shared misreading, which reviewing the same code cannot provide
explanation: A reviewer reading the code can be led down the same path its author was. Independent reproduction is the only one of these that does not share that starting point.

prompt: How do the terms artificial intelligence and machine learning relate to each other?
optionA: Artificial intelligence is one way of doing machine learning
optionB: Machine learning is one way of building artificial intelligence
optionC: The two name the same thing
optionD: The two are separate fields with nothing in common
correctAnswerText: Machine learning is one way of building artificial intelligence
explanation: Machine learning sits inside the wider field, as one approach among several. Rule-based systems are artificial intelligence too and involve no learning at all.

prompt: Where does deep learning sit in relation to machine learning?
optionA: Outside it, as a separate discipline
optionB: Above it, containing machine learning as a part
optionC: Alongside it, with neither containing the other
optionD: Inside it, as one particular approach
correctAnswerText: Inside it, as one particular approach
explanation: Deep learning is a kind of machine learning, so it is the innermost of the three terms. Plenty of machine learning uses nothing that would be called deep.

prompt: A system is described as artificial intelligence. What follows about how it was built?
optionA: Nothing; it may have been written as rules or learned from examples
optionB: That it learned from examples
optionC: That it uses deep learning
optionD: That it was written as a set of rules
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it may have been written as rules or learned from examples
explanation: The term describes what a system does rather than how it was made. Assuming learning from the label is the commonest error in the topic.

prompt: Which ordering places the three terms correctly from widest to narrowest?
optionA: Deep learning, machine learning, artificial intelligence
optionB: Machine learning, artificial intelligence, deep learning
optionC: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning
optionD: Artificial intelligence, deep learning, machine learning
correctAnswerText: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning
explanation: Each term names a subset of the one before it. Reversing the order is what happens when the most recently encountered term is assumed to be the largest.

prompt: A student says that because a chess program plays extremely well, it must be using machine learning. What is wrong with the reasoning?
optionA: Nothing; strong performance does indicate learning
optionB: Playing well says nothing about origin; a program can search possibilities using written rules and never learn
optionC: Chess programs are not artificial intelligence at all
optionD: Chess programs use deep learning rather than machine learning
correctAnswerText: Playing well says nothing about origin; a program can search possibilities using written rules and never learn
explanation: Some chess programs learn and some search using rules written by people, and both play well. Capability and construction are separate questions.

prompt: A thermostat switches the heating on whenever the temperature drops below a figure someone set. Was its behaviour written or learned?
optionA: Learned, because it responds to its surroundings
optionB: Learned, because it acts without being told each time
optionC: Neither; the behaviour has no origin
optionD: Written, because someone stated the condition
correctAnswerText: Written, because someone stated the condition
explanation: Responding to the world is not the same as having learned from it. Every part of what this device does was decided by a person in advance.

prompt: A system was shown thousands of photographs already marked as cats or dogs, and can now sort new photographs. Was its behaviour written or learned?
optionA: Learned, because it was derived from the marked examples
optionB: Written, because someone chose the categories
optionC: Written, because someone assembled the photographs
optionD: Neither, since photographs are not instructions
correctAnswerText: Learned, because it was derived from the marked examples
explanation: People supplied the examples and the categories; nobody wrote down what distinguishes a cat from a dog. That distinction came out of the examples, which is what learning means here.

prompt: A spell checker compares each word against a stored list and flags anything absent from it. Was its behaviour written or learned?
optionA: Learned, because the list came from real text
optionB: Learned, because it improves as words are added
optionC: Written, because the check was stated and the list supplied
optionD: Written for common words and learned for the rest
correctAnswerText: Written, because the check was stated and the list supplied
explanation: The list is data the check consults rather than examples anything generalised from. Adding a word extends the list and changes no behaviour that was not already there.

prompt: Two systems both recommend films. One applies a stated rule that anyone who liked a film is shown others of the same genre. The other derived its suggestions from what viewers went on to watch. What separates them?
optionA: Nothing; both recommend films and are therefore the same kind of system
optionB: Where the behaviour came from: one was stated in advance and the other derived from examples
optionC: The second is artificial intelligence and the first is not
optionD: The quality of their recommendations
correctAnswerText: Where the behaviour came from: one was stated in advance and the other derived from examples
explanation: Both may recommend well or badly, and that is not the question. One does what somebody wrote and the other does what its examples supported.

prompt: A system was trained on a large collection of examples. What were the examples for?
optionA: Building a store the system searches when a question arrives
optionB: Filling a list of answers to give back later
optionC: Testing behaviour that had already been written
optionD: Deriving behaviour that extends beyond the examples themselves
correctAnswerText: Deriving behaviour that extends beyond the examples themselves
explanation: The examples shape the system during training and are not consulted afterwards. Treating them as a store the system looks things up in is the model most students start with.

prompt: After training is finished, does a system still hold the examples it was trained on?
optionA: Not as a collection it can consult; what remains is what was derived from them
optionB: Yes, and it searches them for each new question
optionC: Yes, and it returns whichever example is closest
optionD: No, and so it can no longer do anything
correctAnswerText: Not as a collection it can consult; what remains is what was derived from them
explanation: What survives training is the derived behaviour rather than the material it came from. That is why a trained system can answer about cases its examples never contained.

prompt: A team doubles the number of examples used to train a system. What does this most directly change?
optionA: How quickly the system answers a question
optionB: How much storage the finished system occupies
optionC: What the system derives, and therefore how it behaves
optionD: Nothing, since behaviour is written separately
correctAnswerText: What the system derives, and therefore how it behaves
explanation: More examples give more to generalise from, so the behaviour that comes out of training differs. Speed of answering afterwards is a separate matter.

prompt: A student explains that a trained system works by finding the training example most like the new input and copying its answer. What is wrong with that account?
optionA: Nothing; that is exactly how training works
optionB: It describes a lookup, whereas training derives behaviour that handles inputs unlike any example
optionC: It is right except that the system finds the least similar example
optionD: It is right only for systems trained on photographs
correctAnswerText: It describes a lookup, whereas training derives behaviour that handles inputs unlike any example
explanation: Some methods do work by comparing against stored examples, which is what makes this account plausible. It is not what training in general produces, and it cannot explain sensible behaviour on genuinely novel input.

prompt: A task is to decide, for each incoming message, whether it is urgent or routine. What shape of task is that?
optionA: Predicting a quantity
optionB: Grouping without any categories named in advance
optionC: Ordering the messages by importance
optionD: Sorting into named categories
correctAnswerText: Sorting into named categories
explanation: Two named outcomes with every message going into one of them is sorting into categories. Nothing numeric is being estimated.

prompt: A task is to estimate how many minutes a delivery will take, given the distance and the time of day. What shape of task is that?
optionA: Predicting a quantity
optionB: Sorting into named categories
optionC: Grouping without any categories named in advance
optionD: Deciding whether the delivery will be late
correctAnswerText: Predicting a quantity
explanation: The answer is a number on a continuous scale rather than one of a fixed set of labels. Deciding whether it will be late would be a different task built on top of this one.

prompt: A hospital holds scans with no notes attached, and wants a system that sorts them into healthy and unhealthy. Does the data already contain the answers?
optionA: Yes, because the scans themselves show the condition
optionB: Yes, because the two categories have been named
optionC: No; the scans carry no indication of which are which
optionD: It cannot be determined from what is stated
correctAnswerText: No; the scans carry no indication of which are which
explanation: A scan showing a condition is not the same as a record stating it. Somebody would have to go through and mark them before the answers exist as data.

prompt: A company keeps a record of every subscription and whether it was eventually cancelled. It wants to predict which current subscriptions will be cancelled. Does the data already contain the answers?
optionA: No, because nobody set out to record answers
optionB: Yes; the past cancellations are answers, though nobody created them for this purpose
optionC: No, because the answers concern current subscriptions rather than past ones
optionD: Only if the cancellations were recorded with a reason
correctAnswerText: Yes; the past cancellations are answers, though nobody created them for this purpose
explanation: The outcomes were recorded as a by-product of running the business, and that is exactly what makes them usable. Answers do not have to have been created deliberately to be answers.

prompt: A system must work out the tax owed on a salary, using published bands that are stated exactly in law. Which approach fits?
optionA: A learned system, since there is a great deal of salary data
optionB: A learned system, so that it improves over time
optionC: Either; the two would give the same answers
optionD: A written rule, since the calculation is already stated precisely
correctAnswerText: A written rule, since the calculation is already stated precisely
explanation: Learning would approximate a rule that is already known exactly, and would sometimes get it wrong. When the rule can be written down, writing it down is both cheaper and correct.

prompt: A system must decide whether a handwritten digit is a three or an eight. Nobody can state a rule that reliably separates them. Which approach fits?
optionA: A learned system, since the distinction cannot be written down but examples are plentiful
optionB: A written rule listing the shapes each digit may take
optionC: A written rule based on how much ink each digit uses
optionD: Neither; the task cannot be automated
correctAnswerText: A learned system, since the distinction cannot be written down but examples are plentiful
explanation: This is the case learning exists for: the distinction is real, people apply it effortlessly, and nobody can state it. Attempts to write the rule produce long lists of exceptions.

prompt: A system must decide whether a customer qualifies for a refund. The conditions are set out in a published policy, and every refusal must be explained to the customer by citing the clause that applied. The policy states the conditions exactly and every decision must name the clause it rests on. Which approach fits?
optionA: A learned system trained on past refund decisions
optionB: A learned system, with a written rule used to check it afterwards
optionC: A written rule, because only that can name the clause behind each decision
optionD: A learned system, since past decisions are plentiful
correctAnswerText: A written rule, because only that can name the clause behind each decision
explanation: Past decisions exist and would train something workable, and it could not cite a clause. The obligation to explain is what settles the choice here rather than what is achievable.

prompt: A system is trained on photographs of cats and dogs, all taken indoors. What could it learn to tell apart?
optionA: Indoor from outdoor scenes
optionB: Cats from dogs, as far as the photographs show the difference
optionC: Cats from dogs from rabbits
optionD: The age of each animal
correctAnswerText: Cats from dogs, as far as the photographs show the difference
explanation: A system can only pick up distinctions its examples actually contain. Rabbits never appeared and every photograph was indoors, so neither distinction is available.

prompt: A system is trained to sort customer messages using examples written only in English. What can be said about its handling of messages in other languages?
optionA: It will handle them correctly, since the categories are the same
optionB: It will refuse to sort them
optionC: It will treat every one of them as routine
optionD: Nothing was learned about them, since no example contained one
correctAnswerText: Nothing was learned about them, since no example contained one
explanation: The categories being the same does not help, because nothing in training connected those categories to any other language. What such a system does with them is undetermined rather than safe.

prompt: A system is trained to judge job applications, using examples from a company that has only ever hired graduates of three universities. Every example in the training data comes from those three universities and no other. What has the system had the opportunity to learn about applicants from a fourth?
optionA: Nothing, because no example gave it anything to generalise from
optionB: That they are unsuitable, since none was ever hired
optionC: That they are as suitable as any other applicant
optionD: It will decline to judge them
correctAnswerText: Nothing, because no example gave it anything to generalise from
explanation: Absence from the examples is not evidence of unsuitability; it is absence of evidence. The system will nonetheless produce a confident judgement, which is what makes the gap dangerous rather than merely limiting.

prompt: A system sorts photographs of vehicles correctly nine times out of ten on examples like the ones it was trained on. It is now shown a photograph of a vehicle type that never appeared in training. What follows?
optionA: It will be right about nine times out of ten on this one too
optionB: It will report that it does not recognise the vehicle
optionC: Its performance on that photograph does not follow from its performance on the others
optionD: It will always be wrong on this one
correctAnswerText: Its performance on that photograph does not follow from its performance on the others
explanation: A figure measured on one kind of input says nothing about a different kind. The system has no means of noticing that this input is unlike what it saw.

prompt: A system trained on photographs taken in daylight is given one taken at night. What is the most likely behaviour?
optionA: A refusal to answer
optionB: A confident answer that may well be wrong
optionC: A warning that the input is unusual
optionD: The same accuracy as in daylight
correctAnswerText: A confident answer that may well be wrong
explanation: Nothing in ordinary training teaches a system to recognise unfamiliarity, so it answers as readily as ever. The confidence is what misleads the person reading the output.

prompt: A fault detector was trained on recordings from one factory and is deployed in a second with different machinery. It reports no faults for a month, and the team concludes the second factory is running well. The system was never shown a recording from this factory, so a quiet month tells you as much about the system as about the machinery. What should be concluded?
optionA: That the second factory is running well
optionB: That the detector has failed and should be replaced
optionC: That the second factory has fewer faults than the first
optionD: Nothing yet; the silence could equally mean the detector is unable to judge this machinery
correctAnswerText: Nothing yet; the silence could equally mean the detector is unable to judge this machinery
explanation: Two explanations fit the observation equally, and the report alone cannot separate them. Deliberately introducing a known fault would.

prompt: A system is reported as correct on 90 out of every 100 cases. What else is needed before judging whether that is good?
optionA: How the cases were split between the possible answers
optionB: How long the system takes to answer
optionC: How many examples it was trained on
optionD: Which method was used to build it
correctAnswerText: How the cases were split between the possible answers
explanation: A figure alone cannot be judged. If ninety of every hundred cases share one answer, always giving that answer scores the same and is useless.

prompt: A system detects a condition that occurs in 1 case out of every 100, and is correct 99 times out of 100. Is that impressive?
optionA: Yes, since 99 out of 100 is close to perfect
optionB: Yes, provided the system was trained on enough cases
optionC: Not on its own; always answering that the condition is absent would score the same
optionD: No, because 99 is never a good score
correctAnswerText: Not on its own; always answering that the condition is absent would score the same
explanation: The figure matches what a system that detects nothing would achieve, so it carries no evidence that anything is being detected. What matters is performance on the rare case.

prompt: A system sorts messages into two categories, and the cases are split evenly between them. It is correct 90 times out of 100. Because the two categories occur equally often, always naming one of them would score only 50 out of 100. What does the figure establish?
optionA: Nothing, since accuracy figures are never informative
optionB: That the system is doing substantially better than answering without looking
optionC: That the system is correct on 90 per cent of each category separately
optionD: That the system would score 90 on any data it is given
correctAnswerText: That the system is doing substantially better than answering without looking
explanation: An even split makes the baseline 50, so 90 is a genuine improvement on it. It still says nothing about how the errors are distributed between the two categories.

prompt: A trained system is asked why it gave the answer it did, and produces a fluent explanation. What is that explanation?
optionA: A record of the steps the system took
optionB: A proof that the answer was correct
optionC: A summary of the training examples used
optionD: Another output, which may or may not describe what actually happened
correctAnswerText: Another output, which may or may not describe what actually happened
explanation: The explanation was produced the same way the answer was, so it carries no special authority. Nothing in it is a transcript of the system's working.

prompt: A regulator requires that every automated decision be traceable to a stated reason. A team proposes a learned system that scores well. What is the difficulty?
optionA: A learned system produces decisions rather than reasons, so tracing one to a stated reason is not something it can do
optionB: Learned systems are not accurate enough for regulated work
optionC: Learned systems cannot be tested
optionD: There is no difficulty; the system can be asked to explain each decision
correctAnswerText: A learned system produces decisions rather than reasons, so tracing one to a stated reason is not something it can do
explanation: Asking it to explain produces text, not a reason the decision actually rested on. The requirement is about the decision procedure rather than about producing an account afterwards.

prompt: A team wants a trained system to tell them which of its inputs mattered most to a particular decision. Separate techniques exist for estimating that, and the system itself does not record which inputs it relied on. What is the honest position?
optionA: The system can be asked directly and will answer accurately
optionB: The information is unobtainable by any means
optionC: The system cannot supply it directly, though a separate technique can estimate it
optionD: The information is only obtainable by retraining from scratch
correctAnswerText: The system cannot supply it directly, though a separate technique can estimate it
explanation: Neither extreme is right. There is real work on estimating this, and none of it consists of asking the system and believing what it says.

prompt: A speech system works well for most users and poorly for those with a particular regional accent. Its training recordings came from one city. What is the most likely explanation?
optionA: The system is not powerful enough for speech
optionB: That accent was largely absent from the recordings, so little was learned about it
optionC: That accent is inherently harder to recognise
optionD: The affected users are speaking unclearly
correctAnswerText: That accent was largely absent from the recordings, so little was learned about it
explanation: A gap in the examples becomes a gap in the behaviour. Nothing about the accent itself has been shown to be harder; it was simply not represented.

prompt: A team responds to poor performance on one group by collecting ten times more training data, drawn from exactly the same source as before. The new data comes from the same source and so contains the same group in the same small proportion. What will happen?
optionA: The gap will close, because ten times more data is a substantial increase
optionB: The gap will close for large groups and widen for small ones
optionC: Performance will fall for every group
optionD: The gap will remain, because more of the same data does not represent the missing group any better
correctAnswerText: The gap will remain, because more of the same data does not represent the missing group any better
explanation: Volume and coverage are different things, and only coverage was ever the problem. Collecting from a new source, even in smaller quantity, would address it.

prompt: A system trained to spot diseased leaves scores almost perfectly in testing and fails in the field. Every diseased leaf in the training set was photographed against a blue background and every healthy one against a white background. What did it most likely learn?
optionA: To tell the backgrounds apart rather than the leaves
optionB: To recognise disease, with the field conditions being harder
optionC: To recognise leaf shape rather than colour
optionD: Nothing at all, since it fails in the field
correctAnswerText: To tell the backgrounds apart rather than the leaves
explanation: The backgrounds separate the two categories perfectly and are far easier to detect than the disease. A system uses whatever distinguishes its examples, and this distinguished them completely.

prompt: A system predicting which patients need urgent care performs well in testing and badly in use. In the training records, urgent cases had almost always already been given a particular drug, and that drug appears among the inputs. The drug is recorded because the case was urgent, so it is a consequence of urgency rather than a sign of it. What went wrong?
optionA: The training data was too small
optionB: The drug is a genuine early indicator and the system was right
optionC: The system used a field that only becomes available after the decision it is meant to make
optionD: The system was tested on the wrong patients
correctAnswerText: The system used a field that only becomes available after the decision it is meant to make
explanation: In testing, that field is present and the system looks excellent. At the moment a real prediction is needed, it has not been recorded yet, so the signal the system relied on is simply missing.

prompt: A system is measured on the same examples it was trained on and scores perfectly. What does that establish?
optionA: That it will perform perfectly in use
optionB: That it reproduces those examples; nothing about examples it has not seen
optionC: That it was trained for long enough
optionD: That the examples were of high quality
correctAnswerText: That it reproduces those examples; nothing about examples it has not seen
explanation: Reproducing what it was shown is the least demanding thing a trained system can do. The question worth asking is about inputs held back from training.

prompt: A team splits its data, trains on one part and measures on the other, and reports a strong score. They then adjust the system repeatedly, measuring on that same held-back part each time and keeping whatever scores best. The held-back part guided the adjustments and so is no longer material the system has never been exposed to. What is wrong with the reported score?
optionA: Nothing; splitting the data was done correctly
optionB: The split should have been made in the other proportion
optionC: The score is too low rather than too high
optionD: The held-back part has effectively become part of the training, so the score is optimistic
correctAnswerText: The held-back part has effectively become part of the training, so the score is optimistic
explanation: The split was right and what followed undid it. Choosing among many variants by one measurement fits the system to that measurement, which is why a third, untouched portion is kept back.

prompt: A system is measured on data collected six months after its training data, and scores well. A colleague objects that the measurement is invalid because the data is from a different period. Being measured on later data is closer to how the system will actually be used than being measured on data from the same period. Is the objection sound?
optionA: No; measuring on later data is a stronger test rather than a weaker one
optionB: Yes; the two periods must match for the measurement to be valid
optionC: Yes, unless the system is retrained on the later data first
optionD: No, but only if nothing changed between the two periods
correctAnswerText: No; measuring on later data is a stronger test rather than a weaker one
explanation: The worry behind the objection is real for training data and inverted here. A system that holds up on later data has demonstrated something a same-period measurement cannot.

prompt: A team must compare two systems for spotting fraud. Fraud occurs in about one transaction in a thousand. Proportion correct will be about the same for both systems and for a system that declares every transaction genuine. What should they measure instead?
optionA: Proportion correct, measured over more transactions
optionB: How quickly each system reaches a decision
optionC: How the systems perform on the fraudulent cases specifically
optionD: How many transactions each was trained on
correctAnswerText: How the systems perform on the fraudulent cases specifically
explanation: With a rarity like this, the overall figure is dominated by the common case and cannot separate anything. Only performance on the rare cases distinguishes a useful system from an inert one.

prompt: A system is measured on data held back properly and scores 85 out of 100. In use it scores 60. The held-back data was drawn from the same collection as the training data, while the data met in use was not. What best explains the drop?
optionA: The measurement was carried out incorrectly
optionB: The held-back data resembled the training data more closely than real use does
optionC: The system degraded after being deployed
optionD: The system was trained for too long
correctAnswerText: The held-back data resembled the training data more closely than real use does
explanation: Holding data back protects against measuring on what was trained on, and not against the whole collection differing from the world. That is a separate and commoner gap.

prompt: A system must flag transactions that break a compliance rule. The rule is published, exact, and changes twice a year, and every flag must be justified by citing the rule. The rule is stated exactly and each flag must cite it, while learning would approximate it and could cite nothing. Which approach fits?
optionA: A learned system trained on past flagged transactions
optionB: A learned system, retrained twice a year when the rule changes
optionC: A learned system for the common cases and a rule for the rest
optionD: A written rule, updated when the rule changes
correctAnswerText: A written rule, updated when the rule changes
explanation: Changing twice a year is an argument for something easy to edit, not for retraining. Learning here would be an approximation of something already known exactly.

prompt: A team must build a system to spot defective parts from photographs. Inspectors can identify a defect instantly and cannot say what they are looking at. Twenty thousand photographs already marked by inspectors are available. Which approach fits?
optionA: A learned system, since the distinction is real, unstatable, and richly exemplified
optionB: A written rule, developed by interviewing the inspectors at length
optionC: A written rule based on the size of any mark on the part
optionD: Neither; the inspectors should continue to do it by hand
correctAnswerText: A learned system, since the distinction is real, unstatable, and richly exemplified
explanation: Every condition for learning is met: the judgement exists, nobody can state it, and the marked examples are plentiful. Interviewing to extract a rule is exactly what fails when the expertise is not available in words.

prompt: A learned system would score better than a written rule on a task, and any error affects whether a person receives a benefit they are entitled to, with an appeal process that requires the reason for each decision. Being more often right does not help an appeal that has to be answered with a reason. What should be built?
optionA: The learned system, because it is right more often
optionB: The learned system, with a person reviewing every decision
optionC: The written rule, because the appeal process needs a reason and accuracy cannot supply one
optionD: The learned system, with reasons generated for each decision afterwards
correctAnswerText: The written rule, because the appeal process needs a reason and accuracy cannot supply one
explanation: Generating a reason afterwards produces text that did not drive the decision, which is worse than no reason because it looks like one. Human review of every decision removes the benefit of automating at all.

prompt: A task has a rule that is known exactly but has around four hundred clauses interacting in complicated ways. A team proposes learning it from examples instead. Learning would approximate a rule that is already known exactly, so any disagreement between them is the learned system being wrong. What follows?
optionA: Learning is appropriate, since four hundred clauses are too many to write
optionB: The rule should still be written, since every disagreement would be an error introduced for convenience
optionC: Learning is appropriate, provided the examples come from the rule itself
optionD: Neither approach can work at this scale
correctAnswerText: The rule should still be written, since every disagreement would be an error introduced for convenience
explanation: Complexity is an argument for care in implementing the rule and never for guessing at it. Generating examples from the rule to train something less accurate than the rule is effort spent to become wrong.

prompt: Two teams disagree. One proposes a learned system that is right 94 times in 100 and cannot say why. The other proposes a written rule that is right 88 times in 100 and states its reason every time. The task is suggesting which article a reader might enjoy next, and a wrong suggestion costs a reader a few seconds. Which fits?
optionA: The written rule, because a stated reason is always preferable
optionB: The written rule, because 88 and 94 are close enough to be equivalent
optionC: Neither; readers should choose their own articles
optionD: The learned system, because nothing here needs a reason and the errors are cheap
correctAnswerText: The learned system, because nothing here needs a reason and the errors are cheap
explanation: The same trade decided the other way in a benefits decision, and the difference is what an error costs. Preferring explanations regardless of stakes is a rule that ignores the question.

prompt: A tool is described as deriving its behaviour from a collection of past cases, with no conditions written by hand. It behaves oddly on a case unlike anything in that collection. The tool derived everything it does from the collection and nothing was written by hand. What accounts for the odd behaviour?
optionA: The collection contained nothing resembling this case, so nothing determined the behaviour
optionB: A mistake in the conditions somebody wrote
optionC: The tool has begun to learn from the cases it is now meeting
optionD: The tool is refusing to handle the case
correctAnswerText: The collection contained nothing resembling this case, so nothing determined the behaviour
explanation: With nothing written by hand there are no conditions to contain a mistake. The behaviour on an unrepresented case was never determined by anything.

prompt: A supplier describes a product as improving continuously through use. A buyer asks what that means. The description does not say whether behaviour changes on the buyer machine or whether updated versions are supplied periodically. Which question would settle it?
optionA: How many examples the product was originally built from
optionB: Whether the product uses deep learning
optionC: Whether the behaviour changes between updates, or only when a new version is installed
optionD: How accurate the product is at present
correctAnswerText: Whether the behaviour changes between updates, or only when a new version is installed
explanation: Two very different arrangements are consistent with the phrase, and they differ in whether the buyer can reproduce yesterday behaviour. The other questions are reasonable and do not distinguish the two.

prompt: A system is described as combining written conditions with a learned component: the conditions decide the common cases and anything they do not cover is passed to the learned part. A decision must be explained. The conditions can be cited and the learned part cannot, and which of the two handled a given case is recorded. What follows?
optionA: No decision can be explained, since part of the system is learned
optionB: Decisions handled by the conditions can be explained and the rest cannot, and the record says which is which
optionC: Every decision can be explained, since part of the system is written
optionD: The system should be replaced by one or the other
correctAnswerText: Decisions handled by the conditions can be explained and the rest cannot, and the record says which is which
explanation: A mixed system gives a mixed answer, and the record is what makes that answer usable. Treating it as wholly one or the other discards information that is already being kept.

prompt: A product claims to need no training data because it works out of the box. A team must judge the claim. Behaviour that was not derived on the buyer premises was derived somewhere by somebody, or else written by hand. What does the claim actually tell them?
optionA: That the product uses written conditions rather than learning
optionB: That the product will work equally well on any data
optionC: That the product cannot be evaluated
optionD: Only that they need supply no data; the behaviour still came from somewhere and that origin matters
correctAnswerText: Only that they need supply no data; the behaviour still came from somewhere and that origin matters
explanation: Requiring no data from the buyer is a statement about the buyer effort, not about how the product was built. Whether it was trained on material resembling this buyer situation remains the question worth asking.

prompt: An output contains four statements. Which is most likely to be invented?
optionA: A statement that the topic is widely debated
optionB: A named study from 2019 with two authors and a page range
optionC: A statement that more research would be useful
optionD: A statement that the question is difficult to answer
correctAnswerText: A named study from 2019 with two authors and a page range
explanation: Invention produces precise, well-formed detail because that is what the surrounding text calls for. The three vague statements are nearly always safe and nearly always useless.

prompt: What does a fabricated detail typically look like?
optionA: Vague and hedged
optionB: Obviously unusual in wording
optionC: Marked as uncertain by the system
optionD: Specific, correctly formatted and entirely ordinary
correctAnswerText: Specific, correctly formatted and entirely ordinary
explanation: Nothing about a fabricated detail announces itself. It is produced by the same process as a correct one and comes out looking the same.

prompt: An output gives a statistic to one decimal place and attributes it to a named organisation. What follows from the precision?
optionA: Nothing; precision is not evidence about accuracy
optionB: That the figure came from a real source
optionC: That the figure was computed rather than recalled
optionD: That the figure is current
correctAnswerText: Nothing; precision is not evidence about accuracy
explanation: A precise figure is what the sentence needed, whether or not one exists. Precision reads as authority and carries none.

prompt: Which part of an output about a legal question most needs checking before use?
optionA: The general description of how the law works
optionB: The observation that the area is complex
optionC: The section number of the statute it cites
optionD: The suggestion to consult a professional
correctAnswerText: The section number of the statute it cites
explanation: A section number is precise, checkable, and exactly the kind of detail that gets invented. The general description is harder to falsify and easier to verify loosely.

prompt: A student says they can tell fabricated output apart because it sounds less confident. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; confidence is a reliable signal
optionB: Fabricated output is typically as confident as accurate output, since both are produced the same way
optionC: Fabricated output is more confident, so the test is backwards
optionD: Fabricated output cannot be told apart by any means
correctAnswerText: Fabricated output is typically as confident as accurate output, since both are produced the same way
explanation: Manner is not correlated with accuracy in either direction. It can be told apart, by checking the claim against something outside the system.

prompt: Which of these should not be pasted into an external service?
optionA: A published product manual
optionB: A page from the company public website
optionC: An error message from open-source software
optionD: A customer list including names and addresses
correctAnswerText: A customer list including names and addresses
explanation: The customer list belongs to the people in it and to the company. The other three are already public and pasting them discloses nothing.

prompt: A developer wants to paste twenty lines from a private codebase to ask about an error. What decides whether that is acceptable?
optionA: Whether those lines are confidential, rather than how few of them there are
optionB: The number of lines, since twenty is a small extract
optionC: Whether the error is serious
optionD: Whether the developer wrote the lines themselves
correctAnswerText: Whether those lines are confidential, rather than how few of them there are
explanation: A short extract of confidential material is still confidential. Authorship does not transfer ownership when the work was done for an employer.

prompt: Which of these is confidential in a way that pasting would breach?
optionA: A public holiday calendar
optionB: The office opening hours
optionC: A colleague medical certificate
optionD: A published organisational chart
correctAnswerText: A colleague medical certificate
explanation: Information about an identified person health belongs to them. The others are routinely published and concern nobody in particular.

prompt: A developer replaces the customer names in a file with placeholders before pasting it, but leaves the account numbers, dates and amounts. Is the file now safe to paste?
optionA: Yes, since the names have been removed
optionB: No; the remaining fields may still identify people and are themselves confidential
optionC: Yes, provided the placeholders are consistent
optionD: No, because placeholders make the question harder to answer
correctAnswerText: No; the remaining fields may still identify people and are themselves confidential
explanation: Removing names removes one identifier and not the others, and account numbers are sensitive in their own right. Partial removal is where this goes wrong most often.

prompt: A course states: "Assistance of any kind must be acknowledged in a note at the end of the submission." A student used a tool to check their spelling. What does the rule require?
optionA: Nothing, since spelling is trivial
optionB: Nothing, since spelling checkers are standard
optionC: A note only if the tool changed the meaning
optionD: A note acknowledging it, since the rule covers assistance of any kind
correctAnswerText: A note acknowledging it, since the rule covers assistance of any kind
explanation: The rule as quoted admits no exception for how small the help was. Whether the rule should be that broad is a different question from what it says.

prompt: A course states: "You may use any tool to help you understand the material. Submitted code must be your own work." A student used a tool to explain a concept and then wrote the code themselves. What does the rule require?
optionA: Nothing further; understanding was assisted and the submitted work was their own
optionB: A note acknowledging the tool
optionC: Resubmission without the tool having been used
optionD: Nothing, but only if the concept was simple
correctAnswerText: Nothing further; understanding was assisted and the submitted work was their own
explanation: The rule draws its line at the submitted code and explicitly permits help with understanding. This student stayed on the permitted side of it.

prompt: What decides whether assistance needs declaring?
optionA: How much assistance was taken
optionB: Whether the assistance improved the result
optionC: What the work was meant to demonstrate, and what the applicable rule says
optionD: Whether anyone would be able to tell
correctAnswerText: What the work was meant to demonstrate, and what the applicable rule says
explanation: Quantity is not the test and neither is detectability. The purpose of the work and the stated rule are what settle it.

prompt: A workplace has no stated policy on tool use. A developer used a generator for part of a deliverable and says no declaration is needed because nothing requires one. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; without a rule there is no obligation
optionB: The absence of a rule leaves the question open rather than settling it in their favour
optionC: A rule always exists implicitly and forbids it
optionD: The developer should have refused to use the tool
correctAnswerText: The absence of a rule leaves the question open rather than settling it in their favour
explanation: No rule means nobody has decided, which is a reason to ask rather than a permission. Deciding unilaterally in one own favour is what makes the position weak.

prompt: A generated report for a client contains four claims. Which most needs verifying before the report is sent?
optionA: That the industry has grown in recent years
